title: When Does the AI Bubble Pop? Watch Credit Default Swaps and Token Prices
dek: The AI bubble will eventually burst, but current valuations are far below dot-com levels — Nvidia trades at just 15x earnings. The real risk sits in credit markets, where credit default swaps have climbed to historic highs, signalling a possible sharp selloff ahead.
why: Dan Niles offers quantitative markers for judging the AI bubble (token prices, hyperscaler margins) and a distinctive lens (credit markets, Chinese semiconductors) that is practically useful for understanding where this market cycle stands.
who: Fund managers tracking the AI investment cycle, tech-stock investors, and founders who want to understand both the risks and the opportunities in the AI bubble.
skip: The opening small talk and the closing segment about gaming can be skipped; the core content starts at the 4-minute mark.

points.h: Token prices fell 50% while usage rose 2.5x
points.body: Dan Niles points out that judging whether the AI bubble has topped requires watching two core variables: token output and unit price. Since the end of May, competition from open-source models has pushed token unit prices down about 50%, but output over the same period grew 2.5x. As long as volume growth offsets the price decline, industry revenue is still expanding. At the same time, revenue growth at the three big cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) accelerated from 35% in March to 43% in June, with operating margins up about 2 percentage points — a sign the industry's fundamentals remain healthy.

points.h: 4x leverage, not bad positioning, blew up the fund
points.body: The blow-up of the Situational Awareness fund was not caused by wrong positioning but by its use of 4x leverage. If the underlying falls 25%, 4x leverage means a 100% loss, triggering liquidation. This echoes the lesson of Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) in 1998. After hearing about the fund's problems on July 29, Dan Niles judged that a short-term bottom was near, because the fundamentals (growth in token usage) had not deteriorated. He warns that leverage magnifies risk in both directions, and when long and short positions both move against you at once, it can trigger catastrophic selling.

points.h: Hyperscaler cash flow turns negative for the first time
points.body: Even as hyperscaler revenue accelerates and margins improve, the market worries about deteriorating free cash flow. Google's cash flow, for instance, turned negative for the first time since its IPO because of massive AI capex. Dan Niles sees a parallel to the dot-com era: the technology revolution was real, but stocks could still fall 78% (the Nasdaq from 2000 to 2002). He expects strong industry growth over the next year, but once a hyperscaler cuts capex because of debt problems, it could set off a chain reaction.

points.h: Data center politics is the biggest near-term threat
points.body: Dan Niles points out that the biggest near-term risk to AI growth is not demand but political resistance. A Gallup poll shows 71% of people oppose a data center in their own backyard, higher than the 53% who oppose a nuclear power plant. The two parties rarely agree, yet they agree on opposing data centers, especially in red states like Texas. Hyperscalers have failed to effectively promote the jobs and tax revenue data centers bring, while anti-business forces have successfully cast them as a negative. He expects political risk to weigh on the market through the November midterms.

points.h: Chinese semiconductors will break the no-more-cycles myth
points.body: Dan Niles argues that the view that semiconductors are no longer cyclical is dangerous, and China may be the key to breaking that myth. He draws an analogy to Japan in the 1980s and Korea in the 1990s entering the DRAM market with government support and eventually displacing US dominance. Today China's CXMT (Changxin Memory) and YMTC (Yangtze Memory) are expanding fast: CXMT plans to raise monthly capacity from 300,000 wafers to 500,000, and YMTC aims to overtake Samsung and SK Hynix in NAND. For China, semiconductor self-sufficiency matters more than aircraft carriers.

points.h: Agentic AI extends the cycle by at least a year
points.body: Dan Niles sees agentic AI as an entirely new phase, whose start was marked by the launch of the OpenClaw project on January 30 this year. The agentic phase consumes 10-100x more tokens than chat AI, which will keep driving demand growth. He expects the stock market to have at least another year of upside, but warns to watch competition such as Chinese memory chips. He reminds investors to watch the data like a hawk and avoid being either too optimistic or too pessimistic.

points.h: Software faces AI disruption; security and gaming are relatively safe
points.body: Dan Niles believes AI's impact on software is enormous. OpenAI and Anthropic's combined annualized revenue soared from $29 billion at the start of the year to $105 billion seven months later, and that spending must come out of other software budgets. He likes three relatively safe areas: cybersecurity, recording systems, and video games. Recent moves — Salesforce partnering with Anthropic and Workday being acquired by Silver Lake — suggest software stocks may be near a bottom, but valuations in security are already high.

points.h: Credit markets are the AI bubble's early warning system
points.body: Dan Niles stresses that credit markets are the key to judging the AI bubble. He monitors daily the credit default swap (CDS) prices of hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Google and Nvidia, and finds they are already above the North American investment-grade average and at historic highs. Credit investors are more cautious than equity investors, because bond returns are fixed and principal must be protected. AI's massive capex depends on debt financing, and 30-year Treasury yields have risen to their highest since 2007, raising financing costs — which could be the spark that pops the bubble.

71% were against data centers and only 53% were against nuclear power. That's bad, right? I couldn't believe it when I saw it.

I think many investors greatly underestimate what China is doing. And I hear these arguments and I tell myself that this is exactly what people were thinking back in the 1980s when Japan entered the semiconductor industry.
The agent phase uses 10-100 times more tokens than the chat-based AI phase. So, I think you still have a long way to go, at least another year for the stock to go up.

When you have some of the largest companies in the world that generate the largest cash flow that have credit default swaps trading at premiums to North American investment-grade credit default swaps, that tells you about the ability of the capital markets to absorb that.
